summary: Root cause identified with high confidence (0.78): the pricing-engine config change cfg-3120, which at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z ramped flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100, moved all quote traffic onto the CPU-bound GreeksV2Calculator Monte-Carlo path (~20k paths, 2.9-8.7s per quote). pricing-engine CPU stepped from ~39-41% to ~99% and held, request_rate stayed flat, its own error_rate stepped to ~13%, and p99 went 60ms -> ~2600ms, so order-service quote calls exceeded their 2500ms budget and returned 8% 5xx. The alternative single-change candidate, the market-data-service protobuf deploy dep-6111 at 11:56Z, is outside the onset window and its broader consumer footprint (MDS, api-gateway, portfolio-service) shows no anomaly. Shared redis-cache degradation was ruled out as the mechanism because a blocked-on-cache wait would predict flat CPU rather than the observed load-independent CPU saturation and in-process Monte-Carlo error logs. Residual uncertainty is limited to the flag's runtime effect and 120s telemetry resolution.

ranked_hypotheses.title: pricing-engine Greeks v2 flag ramp (cfg-3120) puts an expensive Monte-Carlo path on all traffic, saturating CPU and stalling quotes
ranked_hypotheses.statement: cfg-3120 ramped flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100 at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z on pricing-engine, moving all quote traffic onto the GreeksV2Calculator Monte-Carlo path (~20k paths, 2.9-8.7s per quote given CPU saturation). pricing-engine CPU steps from ~39-40% to ~99-100% and p99 steps from ~60ms to ~2600ms; order-service quote calls exceed their 2500ms budget and 5xx. Origin is the flag change on pricing-engine, whose new code path is CPU-bound.

causal_chain.claim: cfg-3120 ramps flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5->100 on pricing-engine at 12:04:00Z; it is the only change inside the 12:03-12:06 onset window and lands on the exact service whose p99 stepped

At 5% the v2 path is a small share of quote traffic; at 100% every quote instantiates the expensive Monte-Carlo calculator (open detail: whether the ramp's runtime effect was immediate and whether 5% already consumed the same CPU headroom)
pricing-engine CPU steps from ~39-40% (11:57-12:03) to ~98.95-99.25% in the 12:05 bucket and holds ~98-100% through 13:57
The CPU rise is not load-driven: request_rate is flat at ~582-741 req/s with no step at 12:03/12:06, and memory/restarts are flat (no OOM/restart signature)

pricing-engine logs name the hot path: WARN 'GreeksV2Calculator: Monte-Carlo paths=20000 took <n>ms' (2.9-8.7s per quote, first 12:05:21Z) and ERROR 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2' (first 12:06:41Z), and pricing-engine's own error_rate steps in the same bucket as CPU/latency (0.23% -> 13.01%)

pricing-engine p99 steps 60ms -> ~1739ms avg/2849ms max in the 12:03 bucket and plateaus ~2600ms with no recovery; order-service quote calls then time out at 2500ms with no parse/connection error, driving order-service 5xx to ~8%

assumptions: The 5->100 ramp actually took effect at runtime; no rollout-event row was retrievable, though the change plane shows it remained at 100% (F13).

The CPU burn comes from the Greek v2 compute itself rather than a spin/lock wait induced by v2; pricing-engine exposes no GC/lock/thread metric to separate these (the Monte-Carlo log duration F23 is the only direct evidence and matches CPU-bound compute).
120s bucket resolution means the CPU step (12:03->12:05) cannot be shown to the second to follow the 12:04:00Z ramp, though it is bounded on both sides by it.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared redis-cache degradation stalls pricing-engine quote lookups
ranked_hypotheses.statement: redis-cache (shared:true, used by pricing-engine and market-data-service on the quote path) degraded around 12:00-12:06 (evictions, cold-cache miss storm, or latency), so pricing-engine quote requests wait on cache reads and p99 steps to ~2600ms, propagating up to order-service quote timeouts. Origin is the shared cache, not the flag or the deploy.

causal_chain.claim: redis-cache is a shared dependency of pricing-engine (and market-data-service) with has_telemetry=true, sitting on the quote path

redis-cache degraded around 12:00-12:06 (cold cache / latency / evictions); this is topology-plus-precedent only -- no redis metric value (latency, evictions, hit/miss, connection errors, failover) was ever retrievable (F26) and no redis config change (F27) or restart/redeploy (F28) was recorded
pricing-engine quote lookups block on cache, p99 steps to ~2600ms from the 12:03-12:06 buckets onward (would predict flat pricing-engine CPU and no Monte-Carlo-specific log)
order-service quote calls exceed the 2500ms client timeout and 5xx at ~8%

assumptions: redis-cache actually degraded at onset; no redis telemetry was obtained, so 'no data' is being treated as compatible with degradation (F26: the data source is effectively unavailable).
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: The new telemetry removes this hypothesis: a blocked-on-cache wait predicts flat pricing-engine CPU, but CPU steps to ~99-100% and holds (F19) while request_rate stays flat (F20) -- load-independent CPU burn, not a wait. pricing-engine's own error_rate steps in the same bucket (F22) and its logs name an in-process compute path (Monte-Carlo 'GreeksV2Calculator', 2.9-8.7s, F23), which a cache stall would not produce. No redis config change (F27) or restart/failover event (F28) exists in the window; the only support was a 2025 precedent (F29).

ranked_hypotheses.title: market-data-service protobuf serialization change (dep-6111) degrades downstream consumers
ranked_hypotheses.statement: market-data-service v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf' (dep-6111, 11:56Z) changed the quote payload format; consumer-side handling in pricing-engine would then be expensive (re-parse/re-encode, per-field overhead, larger payloads), stalling its quote handling and stepping p99 to ~2.6s, which makes order-service quote calls exceed their 2500ms budget. Origin is the serialization change.

causal_chain.claim: market-data-service deploys protobuf serialization at 11:56Z (dep-6111), the only deployment in 11:30-12:20, status live, not rolled back
Downstream consumers of the new payload format pay a per-request cost handling it (assumed: the consumer is the bottleneck, since MDS-side telemetry is flat)
pricing-engine p99 steps ~60ms -> ~2600ms and plateaus with no recovery
order-service quote calls exceed the 2500ms timeout, producing ~8% 5xx; no parse/deserialization error appears in the logs

assumptions: This is the reporter's suspicion, retained even though evidence is weak.
MDS payload growth inflates consumer-side work -- untestable, no payload-size/GC metric exists.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: MDS itself shows no anomaly (CPU flat ~44-47%, p99 flat ~39-40ms, errors ~0.2%, no restart: F4/F15) yet was never rolled back; the error signature is timeout-only with zero parse errors (F5); the deploy precedes the first pricing-engine slow-Monte-Carlo log by ~9 minutes and the 12:04 flag ramp sits inside the onset window while dep-6111 is outside it (F14/F24); other MDS consumers (api-gateway, portfolio-service) show no anomaly (F16); and the named hot path is pricing-engine-local compute (F23), not payload handling.

ranked_hypotheses.title: order-service-side saturation/retry amplification inflates quote latency
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The fault originates in order-service (connection/thread-pool exhaustion on the pricing-engine client, or retry amplification): its quote path saturates, its client-side timeouts and 8% 5xx are self-inflicted, and pricing-engine p99 is partly a downstream observer of the retry storm.

causal_chain.claim: order-service shows a sustained step in 5xx to ~8% from the 12:03 bucket
order-service quote-path resources (pool/threads) saturate, or retries amplify load (assumed; no order-service resource metrics were queried)
The only error signature is a client-side timeout to pricing-engine at 2500ms

assumptions: pricing-engine's own CPU saturation, error step and Monte-Carlo log would have to be explained independently or as a retry artifact.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: pricing-engine has its own independent fault signature that cannot be an order-service artifact: CPU step to ~99-100% with flat request_rate (F19/F20), own error_rate step to ~13% (F22), and in-process Monte-Carlo compute logs of 2.9-8.7s (F23). Moreover order-service call volume reaching pricing-engine stayed flat (F20), contradicting a retry storm.

facts.statement: cfg-3120 ramped flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100 ('Ramp Greeks v2 experiment to all traffic') on pricing-engine at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z, and re-querying pricing-engine config changes for 11:30-13:00 returned the same single change, so it remained at 100%.
pricing-engine CPU stepped from ~39-41% (11:45-12:03 baseline) to ~98.95-99.25% between the 12:03 and 12:05 buckets and held ~98-99% (many buckets max 100.0) through 13:57.
pricing-engine request_rate stayed flat (~582-741 req/s; 12:03 avg 644.38, 12:06 avg 658.39), so the CPU jump was not load-driven.
pricing-engine memory_pct stayed flat (46-54%) and restarts was 0.0 in every one of the 45 buckets - no OOM/restart signature.
pricing-engine's own error_rate stepped in the same bucket as CPU/latency (12:03 avg 0.23% -> 12:06 avg 13.01%), plateauing ~12-13% through 13:57.

pricing-engine logs name the hot code path: WARN 'GreeksV2Calculator: Monte-Carlo paths=20000 took <n>ms' (342 occurrences, first 12:05:21Z, durations 2.9-8.7s) and ERROR 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2' (276 occurrences, first 12:06:41Z).

pricing-engine p99 latency rose from a ~59-60ms baseline to ~1739ms avg / 2849ms max in the 12:03 bucket and plateaued ~2600ms; the order-service 180s-bucket p99 confirms the step between 12:03 and 12:06 (151.89ms -> 2840.51ms).
order-service quote timeouts ('pricing-engine quote call timed out after 2500ms') first appear at 12:06:10Z and continue to at least 13:58:24Z (225 ERROR occurrences).
order-service error_rate jumped from ~0.2% baseline to avg 4.15 / max 8.37 in the 12:03 bucket and held a ~8.0-8.3% plateau through the end of the window.
The only error signature on the order-service quote path is a client-side TIMEOUT to pricing-engine; there are zero serialization/parse-error or connection-refused entries.

The only deployment across all services between 11:30 and 12:20 was market-data-service v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf' (dep-6111) at 11:56:00Z; status live, rolled_back_at null, and a wider 11:00-13:59 re-query returned the same single deployment.
market-data-service shows no anomaly in 11:45-13:59: CPU flat ~44-47%, p99 flat ~39-40ms, error_rate flat ~0.2%, no GC/restart anomaly.
redis-cache has no config change in the onset window (scoped audits for 11:30-12:30 and 10:00-13:00 both returned count 0, partial:false) and zero deployments for 11:00-13:59.

No redis-cache metric series were returned by any query; no latency, eviction, hit/miss, connection-error or failover/restart metric value appears in any result, so the redis internal telemetry data source is effectively unavailable.
The quote path is order-service -> pricing-engine -> market-data-service, and redis-cache is a shared platform-owned dependency of both market-data-service and pricing-engine.

Historical precedents are leads only: HIST-113 (2026-01-28 pricing-engine CPU saturation at market open, symptoms 'quote timeouts','cpu 99%') and HIST-107 (2025-12-09 cold cache storm after redis failover); no prior incident involved a serialization/schema change requiring coordinated consumer updates.

assumptions: The 5->100 ramp actually took effect at runtime; no rollout-event or runtime-evaluation row was retrievable, though the change plane shows cfg-3120 remained at 100% (F13).

The CPU burn is caused by Greeks v2 compute itself rather than a spin/lock wait induced by v2; pricing-engine exposes no GC/lock/thread metric to separate these, and the log-derived Monte-Carlo durations (2.9-8.7s) are the only direct mechanism evidence (F23).

Description of the observed onset behavior as a 'step between the 12:03 and 12:05 buckets immediately following the 12:04:00Z ramp' relies on the assumption that the ramp was applied promptly at 12:04 (120s bucket resolution cannot prove sub-2-minute ordering).

The absence of anomalies on api-gateway and portfolio-service (used for the blast-radius argument) rests on the reporting that anomalies appear only on pricing-engine and order-service; those services' telemetry was not directly enumerated in the findings.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) The pricing-engine flag ramp at 12:04:00Z falls inside the onset window (order-service error_rate steps at 12:03 bucket; first quote timeout 12:06:10Z; pricing-engine p99 steps between 12:03 and 12:06) and is the only change in the onset window itself, whereas the MDS deploy at 11:56:00Z is ~8 minutes earlier and outside it.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) Ordering at 120s resolution: pricing-engine CPU and the first GreeksV2Calculator slow-quote log both start between 12:03 and 12:05 (CPU 12:03 avg 39.2 -> 12:05 avg 98.95; first slow Monte-Carlo WARN 12:05:21Z), immediately after the 12:04:00Z ramp and ~2 buckets before order-service's first quote timeout at 12:06:10Z.

timeline.event: market-data-service v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf' (dep-6111) deployed by v.rao; status live, never rolled back. MDS telemetry stays flat afterwards.
Start of onset bucket: order-service error_rate jumps from ~0.2% to avg 4.15 / max 8.37; pricing-engine p99 begins rising (12:03 bucket avg 1739ms). pricing-engine CPU still ~39.2% in this bucket.

cfg-3120 ramps flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100 on pricing-engine ('Ramp Greeks v2 experiment to all traffic'); the only change inside the onset window and on the exact service whose p99 stepped.
pricing-engine CPU saturates: 12:05 bucket avg 98.95 / max 99.25, holding ~99% thereafter. First WARN 'GreeksV2Calculator: Monte-Carlo paths=20000 took <n>ms' at 12:05:21Z (durations 2.9-8.7s).

pricing-engine p99 plateaus ~2600ms and its own error_rate steps to avg 13.01% / max 13.61% in the same bucket; order-service 180s-bucket p99 steps 151.89ms -> 2840.51ms; request_rate remains flat (~658 req/s).

First pricing-engine ERROR 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2' (276 occurrences through 13:58:55Z).
Incident INC-011 [SEV-2] 'Order quotes timing out' reported by on-call SRE, attributed at report time to the market-data-service serialization change.

Conditions unchanged at end of data window: order-service error_rate avg 8.29%, pricing-engine CPU avg 99.33%, pricing-engine error_rate avg 12.56%, request_rate 643.63 req/s - a sustained plateau, not a transient.

recommended_actions.action: Immediately roll back / disable the Greeks v2 flag on pricing-engine by reverting cfg-3120: set flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct back to 5 (or 0) and confirm the change plane shows the new value applied.
recommended_actions.rationale: cfg-3120 (5->100 at 12:04:00Z) is the only change inside the onset window (12:03-12:06) and lands on the exact service whose CPU saturated to ~99% and whose p99 stepped 60ms -> ~2600ms; ordering is bounded on both sides by the last flat sample (12:03) and the first saturated sample (12:05). Reverting is the minimal, targeted mitigation and doubles as the discriminating test between H2 and H3.

recommended_actions.action: Within ~5 minutes of the revert, verify pricing-engine CPU drops back toward ~40%, p99 returns to ~60ms, pricing-engine error_rate returns to ~0.2%, and order-service 5xx returns to ~0.2% / quote timeouts stop.
recommended_actions.rationale: The observed state is a sustained plateau with no recovery (CPU ~99%, p99 ~2600ms, order-service 5xx ~8%, error logs continuing to 13:58). A step-down on revert confirms the flag as the causal driver; continued saturation after revert would falsify H2 and require re-opening H3.

recommended_actions.action: Do NOT roll back market-data-service dep-6111 (protobuf) as the fix; keep it live. If any rollback is contemplated as a precaution, treat it as an independent experiment with its own before/after measurement.
recommended_actions.rationale: MDS shows no anomaly (CPU flat ~44-47%, p99 flat ~39-40ms, errors ~0.2%, no restart) despite the deploy being live, the only error signature is a timeout with zero parse errors, the deploy precedes onset by ~8 minutes and sits outside the onset band, and the MDS payload change would predict anomalies on api-gateway and portfolio-service that were not observed.

recommended_actions.action: Once mitigated, fix forward on the Greeks v2 path: profile/reduce the Monte-Carlo path count (currently 20000 paths taking 2.9-8.7s per quote, against a 2000ms compute budget) or make the v2 path asynchronous/cached so a single quote cannot exceed the 2000ms pricing-engine budget and the 2500ms order-service client budget.
recommended_actions.rationale: The named hot path is GreeksV2Calculator Monte-Carlo with 20000 paths at 2.9-8.7s, which structurally exceeds both the 2000ms in-process budget and the 2500ms caller budget at 100% rollout; the failure mode is per-quote compute cost, not traffic volume (request_rate flat ~645 req/s).

recommended_actions.action: Add capacity/headroom and correctness checks before re-ramping Greeks v2: load-test the v2 path at target request rates to prove CPU headroom, and re-ramp progressively (e.g. 5 -> 25 -> 50 -> 100) with an automated halt if pricing-engine CPU exceeds a defined ceiling or p99 exceeds a fraction of the 2000ms budget.
recommended_actions.rationale: The 5->100 all-at-once ramp moved all traffic onto a path whose measured per-quote cost (2.9-8.7s) saturated CPU at ~99% with flat load; staged rollout with a CPU/latency guard would have prevented the incident and prevents recurrence of the same pattern.

recommended_actions.action: Add pricing-engine instrumentation for GC pause, thread-pool/lock contention and queue depth, and add a rollout-event/runtime flag-evaluation signal so flag ramps can be correlated to telemetry to the second rather than only via the change plane at 120s resolution.
recommended_actions.rationale: pricing-engine currently exposes only cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate and restarts, so 'CPU-bound Monte-Carlo compute' cannot be separated from a v2-induced spin/lock wait by metric - only the log-derived Monte-Carlo durations support the compute interpretation. The 120s bucket resolution also bounds but cannot prove the CPU step followed the 12:04:00Z ramp to the second; both limitations are recorded in the residual confidence cap.

recommended_actions.action: Obtain and retain redis-cache internal telemetry (latency, evictions, hit/miss ratio, connection errors, failover/restart events) for pricing-engine's quote path; the component is flagged has_telemetry=true but no metric series could be retrieved during this incident.
recommended_actions.rationale: The redis hub hop sits on the quote path (pricing-engine -> redis-cache) and was contradicted on mechanism rather than on redis-side data: a blocked-on-cache wait predicts flat CPU, whereas CPU saturated independently of load with pricing-engine's own error_rate stepping in the same bucket and logs naming an in-process compute path; redis is also clean on the change plane (no config changes, no deployments). Restoring this data source closes the last untestable alternative for future incidents.

recommended_actions.action: Add a guardrail/canary policy for all config-flag ramps that switch hot compute paths on shared services: require staged ramp plus automatic rollback on CPU-saturation or error-rate step, and surface flag changes on the same dashboard as service CPU/p99/error rate.
recommended_actions.rationale: The config-change audit for all services in 11:30-12:20 was itself incomplete (shard 2/3 did not respond), and the decisive change was only found by a later scoped query - a reminder that change visibility plus automated guardrails, not manual correlation, is required to prevent recurrence of a flag-driven saturation event.

data_gaps: No runtime rollout-event or flag-evaluation row exists for cfg-3120 - only the change plane showing flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct at 100% after 12:04:00Z. It is therefore assumed, not verified, that the ramp actually took effect at runtime and moved all traffic onto the Greeks v2 path.

pricing-engine's finest available CPU/latency resolution is 120s buckets, so the CPU step can only be bounded to the 12:03-12:05 window; it cannot be shown to the second that the CPU step follows (rather than coincides with) the 12:04:00Z ramp.

pricing-engine exposes no GC, thread-pool, lock-contention or queue-depth metric (only cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts), so 'CPU-bound Monte-Carlo compute' cannot be separated by metric from a v2-induced CPU-burning spin/lock wait; the log-derived Monte-Carlo durations (2.9-8.7s) are the only direct mechanism evidence.

redis-cache has has_telemetry=true but no metric series (latency, evictions, hit/miss, connection errors, failover/restart) was retrievable by any query, so H3 was contradicted on mechanism and change-plane evidence rather than on redis-side metric data; 'no redis anomaly' cannot be distinguished from 'no redis data'.

The all-services config-change audit for 11:30-12:20 was incomplete ('config-audit shard 2/3 did not respond', partial:true), so it cannot be proven that no other service or shared-component owner made a coincident config change in the onset window.

market-data-service response size/payload bytes and GC metrics are not exposed (only cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts), so whether the protobuf change inflated response size or consumer-side parsing cost could not be tested directly; it was refuted only via flat MDS telemetry, the timeout-only error signature, blast radius and timing.

Historical precedent search specifically about serialization/schema changes requiring coordinated consumer updates returned budget_exhausted and was never executed, and a pricing-engine both-direction dependency query also returned budget_exhausted, so pricing-engine's upstream callers and any additional attached shared components beyond those seen via order-service/market-data queries remain unenumerated.

The blast-radius argument (no anomalies on api-gateway or portfolio-service, which the MDS payload change would also affect) rests on the reported anomaly set rather than direct per-service telemetry enumeration in the findings.
No confirmation of the eventual outcome exists: the natural confirmation of the top hypothesis (step-down of CPU/p99/errors on flag revert) is outside the current incident window.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Reverting cfg-3120 (greeks_v2 rollout back to 5 or 0) does NOT bring pricing-engine CPU back toward ~40%, p99 back to ~60ms and order-service 5xx back to ~0.2% - that would falsify H2 and re-open H3 or an unidentified cause.

Retrievable redis-cache telemetry showing a latency step, eviction storm, hit/miss collapse or failover/restart at ~12:00-12:06Z - that would restore the shared-cache degradation hypothesis and point at a different fix.

A runtime flag-evaluation/rollout event proving the 5->100 ramp did not take effect at 12:04:00Z (or took effect materially later), which would remove the temporal link between the change and the onset.

Evidence that the CPU burn is a v2-induced spin/lock or downstream wait rather than Monte-Carlo compute (e.g. GC pauses, lock contention, blocked downstream spans) - this would change the remediation from 'reduce Monte-Carlo cost / stage the ramp' toward dependency or concurrency fixes.

A subsequent anomaly appearing on api-gateway, portfolio-service or market-data-service consistent with the protobuf payload change, or evidence that MDS responses grew in size - this would revive H1 as a contributing or independent cause.

A coincident config or deployment change on another service or shared component (redis-cache, ledger-db, kafka, exchange-gateway) in the 12:00-12:20Z window, which the incomplete all-services config audit could have missed and which would re-open the origin attribution.
Evidence that pricing-engine request volume or client retry amplification actually did rise at onset (contradicting the flat request_rate), which would revive H4 as a contributing factor.

findings.statement: The quote path is order-service -> pricing-engine -> market-data-service (caller->callee http edges), so both order-service and pricing-engine are direct/indirect consumers of market-data-service; market-data-service is additionally called by api-gateway and portfolio-service.

Shared components on/around the affected path: redis-cache (type redis, owner platform, shared:true) is used by both market-data-service and pricing-engine; order-service also depends on the shared ledger-db (postgres, shared:true) and shared kafka (queue-produce, shared:true). Any of these could propagate failure into the quote path.

Historical search found no incident involving a serialization/schema change or coordinated consumer updates; closest precedents are HIST-113 (2026-01-28 pricing-engine CPU saturation at market open, symptoms 'quote timeouts','cpu 99%', cause capacity_saturation) and HIST-107 (2025-12-09 cold cache storm after redis failover, services redis-cache+market-data-service, symptom 'quote latency'). These are leads only; different causes are documented for each.

A pricing-engine config/feature-flag change exists that neither T1 nor T2 had: cfg-3120 ramps 'flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct' from 5 to 100 ('Ramp Greeks v2 experiment to all traffic') at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z, on pricing-engine itself. Re-querying pricing-engine config changes for 11:30-13:00 returns the same single change, so it remained at 100%.

Timing fit: the pricing-engine flag ramp at 12:04:00Z falls INSIDE the onset window (order-service error_rate steps at the 12:03 bucket; order-service quote timeouts first log 12:06:10Z; pricing-engine p99 steps between the 12:03 and 12:06 buckets). It is the only change in the onset window itself; the market-data-service deploy at 11:56:00Z is 8 minutes earlier and outside it. The change lands on the exact service whose p99 stepped (60ms -> ~2600ms).

A market-data-service-side fault during the onset window is contradicted by T1's flat MDS telemetry (CPU ~44-47%, p99 ~39-40ms, errors ~0.2%, no GC/restart anomaly) and by the absence of any MDS-side error, yet protobuf was 'live' and not rolled back. If the serialization change were the direct driver, MDS-side latency/CPU/errors would be expected to move; they did not.

Blast-radius / affected-service set: the two candidate changes touch different service sets. The MDS protobuf payload change is consumed by market-data-service's callers (pricing-engine, api-gateway, portfolio-service) and would predict latency/errors on ALL of those consumer services; the pricing-engine Greeks v2 flag affects only pricing-engine and its downstream caller order-service. T1 reports anomalies only on pricing-engine and order-service (no MDS, no api-gateway/portfolio anomaly), which matches the flag's narrower footprint rather than the MDS payload's broader consumer footprint.

Shared-component path: pricing-engine depends on market-data-service (http) and on shared redis-cache; market-data-service also depends on redis-cache. So a redis-cache degradation could in principle propagate into pricing-engine, but T1 found no redis-cache-side anomaly report and no rollback or cache event was recorded. redis-cache is therefore a shared component that CANNOT be excluded purely on topology and should be checked for telemetry.

Historical precedents are leads only and do not support the MDS-serialization hypothesis: searches returned no incident involving a serialization/schema change requiring coordinated consumer updates. Closest hits are HIST-113 (pricing-engine CPU saturation at market open, symptoms 'quote timeouts','cpu 99%') and HIST-107 (cold cache storm after redis failover involving redis-cache+market-data-service), plus HIST-101 (bad deployment auth-service, bcrypt cost raised). HIST-113 in particular is a pricing-engine-side precedent for the same top-line symptom.

findings.statement: pricing-engine CPU does NOT stay flat: cpu_pct sits at ~39-41% through the 11:45-12:03 baseline (11:57 avg 40.08, 12:00 avg 40.31) and steps to CPU saturation coincident with the p99 step: 12:05 bucket avg 98.95 / max 99.25, 12:07 avg 99.05, and holds ~98-99% (many buckets max 100.0) for the rest of the window through 13:57 (avg 99.33, max 100.0). The step lands between the 12:03 bucket (avg 39.2) and 12:05 bucket (avg 98.95) at 120s resolution.

pricing-engine request_rate stays FLAT across the onset: ~582-741 req/s throughout, with no step at 12:03/12:06 (12:00 avg 648.68, 12:03 avg 644.38, 12:06 avg 658.39, 13:57 avg 643.63; summary mean 645.8). Traffic volume did not rise, so the CPU jump is not load-driven.

pricing-engine memory_pct and restarts are FLAT: memory hovers 46-54% with no trend across the step (12:00 avg 49.89 -> 12:06 avg 48.44, 13:57 avg 48.54), and restarts is 0.0 in every one of the 45 buckets (summary min 0.0 max 0.0). No OOM/restart-crash signature.

pricing-engine's own error_rate steps in the SAME bucket as CPU/latency: ~0.18-0.25% through 12:03 (12:03 avg 0.23), then 12:06 avg 13.01 / max 13.61, plateauing ~12.0-13.1% to 13:57 (avg 12.56). Combined with F3 this shows the fault is inside pricing-engine, not only a blocked wait.

pricing-engine logs name the exact hot code path: the only two patterns are WARN 'GreeksV2Calculator: Monte-Carlo paths=20000 took <n>ms' (342 occurrences, first 12:05:21Z, e.g. 6465ms, 8361ms, 8710ms) and ERROR 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2' (276 occurrences, first 12:06:41Z), spanning 12:05:21Z-13:58:55Z. Monte-Carlo compute itself takes 2.9-8.7s per quote, consistent with 100% CPU and the 2500/2600ms deadline overruns.

findings.statement: Ordering at 120s resolution: pricing-engine CPU + the GreeksV2Calculator slow-quote log both start between 12:03 and 12:05 (CPU 12:03 bucket avg 39.2 -> 12:05 avg 98.95; first slow Monte-Carlo WARN 12:05:21Z), i.e. immediately after the 12:04:00Z cfg-3120 Greeks v2 ramp to 100% and ~2 buckets before order-service's first quote timeout at 12:06:10Z. The flag ramp is bounded by the last flat Greek-v2-free sample (12:03) and the first saturated sample (12:05), so its position vs the 12:04 flag change is consistent but this telemetry cannot resolve finer than 2 minutes.

redis-cache reports has_telemetry=true and is a shared platform-owned redis used by (callers->callee 'cache' edges) auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service, so it sits on the quote path (pricing-engine -> redis-cache).

No redis-cache metric series were returned by any query: the only redis-scoped tool outputs were config/deployment/dependency records, and no latency, eviction, hit/miss, connection-error or failover/restart metric value appears in any result for redis-cache. The data source for redis-cache internal telemetry is effectively unavailable to me.

Config-change audit scoped to redis-cache for the onset window (11:30-12:30Z) and a wider window (10:00-13:00Z) both returned count 0, partial:false -- no flag/config change on the redis component around 12:00-12:20Z.
Deployment audit scoped to redis-cache for 11:00-13:59Z returned zero deployments, partial:false -- no redis restart/failover, rollback or redeploy event was recorded around onset.

The only redis-related event matching H3's described mechanism is a historical precedent: HIST-107 (2025-12-09) 'Cold cache storm after redis failover', services ['redis-cache','market-data-service'], symptoms ['cache miss storm','quote latency'], root_cause 'Redis primary failure promoted an empty replica' (match_score 5.5). This is a past incident, not current telemetry.
